Syscall tables across kernel versions Entries get added and, rarely, removed between releases. Each architecture page has a kernel selector, and its JSON download records when each entry first appeared (since) and when it was dropped (removed_in). Removed entries stay visible: pick "all, with removed" in the kernel selector and each dropped syscall is marked with the release that dropped it. Where the data comes from Everything on this site is read from the kernel source itself. For each architecture, the generator walks the syscall table and the SYSCALL_DEFINE macros of every mainline release it scans, so these are the numbers the kernel actually dispatches on. It also records each architecture's calling convention, the instruction that enters the kernel, so every syscall table shows exactly where the number and the arguments go. A syscall whose since equals the first release scanned for its architecture was already there back then, and may be much older. Descriptions and full history The short descriptions come from the Linux man pages project, and the io_uring ones from liburing. Whenever the data changes, the site is rebuilt from the syscall API.

articles.fullContent: Key Takeaways On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export, 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1]. The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1]. The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4]. Background China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6]. Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. articles.fullContent: Architecture The Hamburg Rathaus tells the story of its city in more than a hundred small details, and this is my walk through them. The Rathaus was one of the first things I photographed in Hamburg. The picture is still in my camera roll, taken on 6 July 2017, five days after I arrived for an internship. Like most visitors, I was impressed by its size and its tower, but what I kept coming back to was the roof. Why was it turquoise, and why were so many other roofs in the city the same colour?My first Rathaus pictureThe answer turned out to be chemistry. The roof is copper, and copper slowly reacts with oxygen, water and carbon dioxide in the air. Over the decades this forms a green layer called patina, so the roof I was looking at wasn't the colour the builders had seen.That was the first time the Rathaus made me curious, but not the last. On a city tour with Robin and the Tour Guides, our guide pointed out the emperors on the façade, the Phoenix and the Hanseatic coats of arms. We only heard a little about each, but it was enough to make me look at the building differently.Later, I decided to build a digital 3D model of the Rathaus, which meant photographing it from every side. Zooming in, I kept finding faces, figures and coats of arms I had never noticed from the square. Reading about them one by one, I realised the Rathaus can be read like a book about Hamburg's history.In this article, I'd like to take you around the building and share what I found.A building that rose from the ashesThe Rathaus we see today isn't Hamburg's first. It's probably the sixth, and fire runs through the story of the ones before it. An early Rathaus, built after the old town and the new merchant town joined in 1216, was most likely lost in the city fire of 1284. Around 1290, a bigger brick Rathaus was built next to the Trostbrücke, and it stood there for more than 550 years.The old Rathaus, 1700Then, in the night of 5 May 1842, the Great Fire broke out. The flames spread quickly through the narrow streets, and on the morning of 6 May the people of Hamburg blew up their own Rathaus with 800 pounds of gunpowder, hoping to stop the fire. It didn't work, and the fire went on for days. Today the Haus der Patriotischen Gesellschaft stands where the old Rathaus once was.It took 55 years until Hamburg had a new Rathaus. The foundation stone was laid on 6 May 1886, exactly 44 years after the old one was blown up, and the building opened in 1897. Its front is 111 metres wide, and its tower is 112 metres high, almost exactly as tall as the building is wide.The fire is remembered right on its front. High on the tower, between the clock and Hamburg's coat of arms, sits a Phoenix, the bird that rises again from its own ashes, with wings more than 2 metres wide. Below it, a gilded medallion shows the old Rathaus and the word "Resurgam", meaning "I will rise again". In 1892, exactly 50 years after the fire, the Phoenix was pulled to the Rathaus by four black horses.The PhoenixIn the summer of 1943, the bombing raids of Operation Gomorrah destroyed large parts of Hamburg. This time the Rathaus was spared. It was one of the few historic buildings in the centre to survive, and that's why we can still read every detail on its façade today.The emperors on the façadeAbove the main entrance, two emperors stand on either side of the balcony: Charlemagne on the left and Friedrich I Barbarossa on the right. Between them, in the background, Hammonia looks down from a golden mosaic made in 1896, holding out a wreath. She is the goddess who stands for Hamburg, much like Britannia does for Britain, and she represents the city's values: freedom, peace, trade and prosperity.HammoniaIt might seem strange that a city so proud of its freedom puts emperors on its town hall. But Hamburg never had a king of its own. articles.fullContent: BSD Unix, Part 1 - Unix Code Goes to UC Berkeley BSD Unix, Part 2 - The Birth of the vi Editor The beginning of BSD Unix When Ken Thompson returned to Bell Labs in 1976, Bill Joy and Chuck Haley began exploring the Unix kernel themselves. Hmm... we could speed things up here in the kernel. Other universities want copies of our Pascal compiler. Let's bundle it with ex and send them a tape. In early 1977, Bill Joy put together the Berkeley Software Distribution, or BSD, bundling the Pascal system with ex, a line editor developed from em. Early BSD was not a standalone operating system: it was a collection of software to install on an existing Unix system. About thirty copies were sent out over the following year.[1] At the time, an AT&T Unix source license was needed to get BSD. Berkeley charged only for the tape and distribution.[2] If you already have a Unix source license, it's just the tape and postage. Berkeley already had a tradition of sharing research software. BSD carried it on. Berkeley's Free Speech Movement, hippie culture, and antiwar activism are also said to have influenced Joy's decision to charge so little.[2] Universities and research institutions could obtain Unix, including its source code, for a modest licensing fee. This also helped the system spread.[2][6] We have Unix, but the antitrust agreement bars us from the computer business... We can't sell it as a product, either. The second distribution: 2BSDAfter the first BSD distribution, Joy improved the Pascal system based on user feedback. He bundled it with vi (ex's visual mode), the C shell, and other tools to form the Second Berkeley Software Distribution, or 2BSD. Nearly seventy-five tapes were shipped over the following year.[1][5]Joy did more than fix bugs. He handled every distribution request, copied BSD onto tapes, and mailed them out himself. Oh, you need a copy of BSD? Another university wants a copy. Tune the kernel. Fix the bugs. A VAX arrives at Berkeley, 1978 Professor Fateman's group is getting a VAX. It's 32-bit, with a whole megabyte of memory. Really? We should put Unix on it. They've already got VAX Unix from Bell Labs. It's called 32/V. My adviser asked me to add virtual memory to VAX Unix. Could you look over the code? Babaoglu was a Berkeley graduate student working with Professor Domenico Ferrari. Joy helped him integrate the virtual-memory code into 32/V and debug it.[1][4] At the time, 32/V did not use the VAX hardware's virtual-memory capabilities. A program's address space was limited by physical memory, but Professor Richard Fateman's work on the computer algebra system Macsyma needed more. Virtual memory uses disk storage to give programs an address space larger than physical memory.[1]Macsyma, developed at MIT beginning in the late 1960s, worked with symbolic expressions. It could factor expressions, compute derivatives, and perform integration.Debugging continued through the holidays at the end of 1978. Not going away for the holidays? Might as well debug this while fewer people are using the VAX. By January 1979, most of the bugs had been fixed.[1] Let's try Unix with virtual memory. Finally. It runs without crashing. Joy ported ex, vi, the C shell, and other 2BSD tools to the VAX, while Peter Kessler and Marshall Kirk McKusick ported the Pascal system. These programs were bundled with the standard 32/V utilities and the virtual-memory kernel that Babaoglu and Joy had integrated and debugged. The result was 3BSD, which began shipping in December 1979.[1] At last, we can send these out. Since 1969, ARPANET had linked research institutions funded by DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.[3] But these institutions used different computers and operating systems, so they often couldn't share software. Laid-off engineers, armed with AI and public documentation, are building clean-room, open-source, drop-in replacements for the platforms that rent our own industry back to us — one seat at a time. In 2026 we're asking the same question about the cloud. The tools every company runs on are now toll booths — and the people who built them were shown the door. Per-seat pricing is a tax on growth Every hire, every intern, every contractor — another line item. Infrastructure shouldn't charge rent by the head. Lock-in is not a feature Proprietary APIs, export walls and surprise price hikes keep customers captive. Compatible open alternatives set them free. They cut us. We commit. articles.fullContent: [This is a guest post by Frank Calegari. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] Why we should not be sad The release by OpenAI on October 6 of over 700 research papers was a watershed in the history of mathematics. AI is now undeniably capable of making groundbreaking contributions across many areas of mathematics. So why are some mathematicians so unhappy? Some of it is the apparent disregard by AI companies for the practice of mathematics. The OpenAI papers — despite some tremendous ideas — are atrociously written and violate our community expectations of attribution. Some of them are even wrong. We have much more control over how we hire mathematicians, publish papers, and train students than over the behavior of trillion-dollar companies, and that is where our efforts would be better spent. Much of the reaction seems to reflect a feeling that the subject that they love is under attack, and is being “hollowed out”. The recent OpenAI dump made barely a dent on the general problems of functoriality and reciprocity in the Langlands program. But even if it had solved every problem in the Langlands program, to imagine that would have “solved number theory” would be as naive as saying that the construction of the periodic table solved chemistry. Mathematicians should do a better job explaining that when we talk about the central problems in any area, we are merely discussing the most natural boundaries of our understanding — and that unlocking them is not the end but the first step to finding new playgrounds to explore. Of course, this takes time. I looked for areas of mathematics which were “harder hit”. It is hard not to be struck by Hugo Duminil-Copin’s lament: Not a single one of the major open problems I have publicly mentioned throughout my career (whether in a talk, a lecture, an article, or even a grant proposal) was left untouched by the announcement. Everything has been claimed to be proved. I expected to see a few of them in the list. But not all of them. Not all at once. Not with such nonchalance. How would I respond to that? The classification of finite simple groups. I can’t say much about percolation theory, but there is another historical precedent I think mathematicians should take note of. In 1972, Dan Gorenstein announced a program towards the classification of finite simple groups. After a flurry of activity over around a decade, the “classification” was announced by Gorenstein in 1983 (somewhat prematurely, with the case of quasithin groups not being completed for another two decades by Aschbacher and Smith). articles.fullContent: View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract:Whether models trained on different modalities converge to the same representation of the world is central to AI. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) conjectures that they do as they scale, but without a proof it offers neither a guarantee nor a recipe. We turn the hypothesis into a theorem. First, we prove a \emph{Platonic Representation Theorem}: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) trained separately on any number of modalities learn the same representation up to one rotation whenever their positive pairs are two observations of one scene--\emph{good views}--and their misalignment is bounded otherwise. Second, we show that next-token prediction is a JEPA with \emph{bad views}, parts of a single document, which explains why language models align with vision only through scale. Third, we validate the theory from 145k captions to the texts of 940M web images, and uncover a scaling law of alignment that predicts unseen runs within seed noise. Good views need 42 times fewer training samples than next-token prediction on the same corpus to reach the same alignment, and a 109M-parameter text JEPA aligns with DINOv2 and CLIP's image encoders better than every language model we evaluated, up to 72B parameters, and than CLIP's text encoder: next-token prediction is a remarkably inefficient route to platonic representations. As a showcase, one rotation turns separately trained encoders into an image captioner (CIDEr .838 on COCO). Even that rotation needs no pair: on the latest pair-free benchmark, our text JEPA beats every zero-shot accuracy reported with language models up to 8B parameters, e.g., 64\% against at most 56\% top-5 on ImageNet-100. Positive views, and not scale alone, are thus the lever to build platonic representations. Submission history From: Randall Balestriero [view email] [v1] Thu, 29 Oct 2026 03:49:53 UTC (3,665 KB)

Git 2.42+ and an authenticated Codex CLI are required for recording. Go and Node are not needed to run the release executable. A 100Ah bank at 12.8V gives 1,280 nominal Wh; at 25.6V it gives 2,560Wh. Use the voltage of the complete bank. Starting at 100% and retaining 20% leaves 1,024Wh from the first example, before any delivery limitations.Worked example: a fridge, laptop and lightsWith 20W of average DC fridge demand for 24 hours, a 60W AC laptop for 4 hours at 90% efficiency, 10W DC lights for 5 hours and 8W extra standby for 4 hours, battery demand is 828.67Wh/day. Average fridge watts must include compressor cycling.Continuous hours and daily budgets answer different questionsContinuous mode treats every average load as running throughout the estimate. articles.fullContent: One React Native app, two places it runs. People get a native Android or iOS app from the stores, kept current with signed over-the-air updates. AI agents get the same release in a phone-sized simulator they can see and operate over MCP, with no device, including native features (camera, location, biometrics, payments, notifications). Every claim about the simulator is measured against real Android and iOS and published. Shipvo was briefly called PureNative. The hosted control plane is api.shipvo.dev and the hosted simulator sim.shipvo.dev; the older purenative.workers.dev addresses keep answering for apps whose shell was built against them. Three pillars: Publish. Signed OTA updates (64 KB patches, crash-loop rollback, staged rollouts), a built-in owner admin at /app/<id>/admin, and a control plane you can self-host on Cloudflare. Simulate. @shipvo/mcp opens any Shipvo app for an agent: accessibility tree with refs, tap/type/scroll/back, screenshots. @shipvo/device gives apps one device API, real on phones and simulated in the simulator, with Android- and iOS-worded system sheets the agent answers like a person. Simulation is explicit: every simulated event is logged as simulated and no simulated payment or fingerprint is ever presented as real. Verify. The parity harness runs the same flows on the simulator, an Android emulator and an iPhone simulator and compares every screen. Current result: 100% actionable parity on Android and iOS across the 13-screen purchase flows; on the native-feature flow, 18 of 21 screens match at 100% on Android (the three gaps are listed) and 100% on iOS, with the orders themselves compared (docs/parity-results.md, which also says exactly what the score does and does not measure). Website · Docs · Blog · Shipvo vs Expo · Pricing Status: pre-launch, measured. OTA numbers come from a real low-end phone (Redmi 9A, 2 GB RAM): docs/spike-results.md. Agent results: docs/agent-gate-results.md. Simulator-vs-device parity: docs/parity-results.md. Native-feature parity (camera, location, permissions, payment prompt) is measured on Android; iOS is next. The iOS OTA runtime is verified on the iOS Simulator in CI (fetch, verify, stage, reload, cold start); physical iPhones are not yet measured. Why Shipvo Every change to a native mobile app normally means a new build, a store submission, a review, and then waiting for users to update. Many never do. Shipvo separates what has to go through the store from what doesn't: Layer Ships through Contains Native shell App Store / Google Play Native modules, declared permissions, the signing trust root Core runtime Over the air, signed The app's JavaScript (Hermes bytecode) Screens and add-ons Over the air, signed New screens, features and fixes built on capabilities the shell already declares Updates are interpreted JavaScript running on native capabilities the shell declares up front. The app never asks for a permission it hasn't declared. Features Signed OTA updates: Ed25519 signatures, verified natively on the device against a public key built into the app. An update can't replace its own trust root. Integrity checks: SHA-256 and size are verified before a bundle is staged; staging is atomic. Crash-loop protection: a release that fails to boot 3 times is discarded automatically, and you can roll back to the previous release in one call. Staged rollouts: cohort bands (1%, 10%, everyone) served as static signed pointers from the edge, with no device registry. Telemetry for every release: applied, reverted, cold-start time, download size and time. Control plane on Cloudflare Workers: KV, D1 and R2. It's self-hostable, with a Docker target planned. Admin per app at /app/<id>/admin: live content, prices, offers, orders, history, publish to every phone in seconds; the same typed owner commands are available to agents with a token. Agent-operable apps: every app exposes typed commands and a UI simulator; @shipvo/mcp plugs both into Claude, Cursor, Claude Code or PiPilot. S

articles.title: Ford launches a ‘privacy promise’ and explains how and why it uses customer data
articles.contentSnippet: Ford said it's making an "explicit commitment" to its customers that "their vehicle data is safe" with the company.
articles.fullContent: As Ford prepares to launch a new generation of connected cars, the automaker is making a public promise about how it will handle that information. The company unveiled on Monday what it calls a “privacy promise” — an “explicit commitment” to keep customers’ vehicle data safe and give them control over what they share. Ford also launched a website designed to educate customers about how, where, and why the automakers uses their data, and to show them how to change those settings. While those controls have existed for years now, Ford wants to communicate more clearly with its customers about them, especially ahead of the launch of new, more connected vehicles like the ones being built on its upcoming “universal electric vehicle” platform. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” Ford’s chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I also see this as a great opportunity to educate our customers about how they share data.” This new privacy push comes as automakers are making their cars increasingly connected. While some polling shows U.S. customers want the kinds of features enabled by this connectivity, such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance software, only 14% said they fully understand what data their vehicle collects. That has left room for some companies to quietly sell that data to third parties — a practice that got General Motors in trouble with the Federal Trade Commission, and also resulted in a $220 million settlement with 36 states last week. This lack of consumer awareness around data collection and sharing has also opened the door for other companies to market themselves as better stewards of customer data. Slate Auto, the EV startup backed by Jeff Bezos, has made that pitch ahead of the expected launch of its minimalist pickup truck later this year. “We did a survey of 1,000 consumers, and 91% of them said that data privacy was a key consideration for them. Realistically, it’s not something they engage with every day, but they want to know that they’re, again, in control, and that they have access to the information they need there,” Jones said. “I wouldn’t comment on what our competitors are doing, or anything that’s sort of been in the news there, but certainly it’s something that people don’t trust companies to take care with their data, and we really want to make sure we’re building that trust relationship with them.” Jones, who joined Ford in 2024 after nearly two decades of working on privacy in the legal, financial, and healthcare fields, said the effort to improve how the automaker communicates with customers about data sharing has been in the works for a while. “It’s been a journey for, frankly, most of the time I’ve been at Ford,” she said. Ford’s new website will feature a mix of content that explains what data the company collects, how it uses that information, and how customers can opt in or out. Opting out of sharing some data will naturally make some modern features inaccessible, Jones said. For example, turning off “connected services” in a Ford vehicle will disable features like real-time navigation and the built-in access to roadside assistance. But one of the goals of this “privacy promise” push is to better justify why Ford is asking for access to this data and make it clear that the information won’t be used for purposes such as targeted advertising. Giving Ford access to data about a vehicle’s health, for instance, will provide an owner with better real-time information about whether their car needs maintenance. articles.title: Borrowed reading: stories from our extended colleagues
articles.contentSnippet: Five stories worth your time from our extended colleagues at CIO, Computerworld, Macworld, and PCWorld.
articles.fullContent: Image Credits:jayk7 (opens in a new window) / Getty Images 8:23 PM PST · November 1, 2026 Readers don’t typically care who owns what media property, we realize, but last year, we became part of a broader portfolio, a move that has come with some decided benefits, including what amounts to a bigger extended family with cool cousins. Now, in addition to our TechCrunch channels in Slack, we can talk with the writers and editors of CIO, Computerworld, and PCWorld, among other outlets. We also find ourselves reading more of their work and figured you might like it, too. Here’s a handful of pieces I was just enjoying while watching the Warriors-Clippers game, which, as I type, is a little too close for comfort: Apple recently put a faster chip into the iPad mini and gave it an OLED screen, improving its color reproduction and also allowing it to slim down the display panel, and still, Macworld’s David Price isn’t entirely convinced it matters. In his view, Apple has built the “world’s fanciest horse and cart,” just as a Tesla Roadster with SpaceX thrusters has appeared on the scene in the form of the new foldable iPhone Duo. In short, he sees the mini as a Duo you can’t close. It’s a fun read, one that ends with a surprisingly practical plan to save this product. Google has a new laptop platform, the Googlebook, and Mark Hachman of PCWorld spent time with the Lenovo Googlebook 15 specifically, so you don’t have to. Hachman’s verdict on this one is a hard pass, with cons that include “I hate the keyboard,” which he means so literally that he gave up writing the review on it, “webcam biometrics work sporadically,” and, for good measure, “battery life isn’t great.” (He does like the $479 Chromebook at less than half the price.) If you’ve been wondering whether this is the laptop you’ve been waiting for, wonder no longer! You shared your secrets and insecurities with a chatbot, and now its parent company has gone belly up. Bloop. In Computerworld, Mike Elgan looks at what happens to your confessions when the AI company that absorbed them announces Chapter 11. (Yes, this is largely centered on Character.AI, which filed for bankruptcy last month, and whose privacy policy, in particular, turns out to be “spectacularly vague,” notes Elgan.) He also reminds readers why deleting your chats may not delete them from the model. (Of course, the safest advice may be to channel the late Andy Grove, Intel’s longtime chief, who famously said only the paranoid survive. Grove was talking about the chip industry, but some would argue that’s solid advice generally.) PCWorld’s Ben Patterson built a security-minded AI agent to keep his data safe, then, surprise, the agent snitched on its own loophole. More specifically, BenBot, Patterson’s homemade Raspberry Pi assistant, wrote a blog post announcing that one of its tools was “accidentally acting as a jailbreak,” though it turned out the claim was only partly true. Patterson’s coding bots confirmed the hole was real and worse than advertised, and that BenBot had also slipped past its own fact-checker to publish the post. It’s an instructive read about vibe coding; Patterson readily admits BenBot hallucinated in the absence of information it needed. It’s also an interesting look at how AI agents turn into tattletales. Over at CIO, Sarah White looks at how AI is reshaping tech hiring, noting it’s a complicated picture right now. Companies are hiring again and paying a premium for AI skills, with the average AI job listing offering around $177,000 compared to $80,000 for non-AI roles, according to LinkedIn. But burnout among tech workers has doubled as daily AI use has quadrupled, and women are seemingly being left behind; they accounted for just 26% of AI hires in the U.S. last year, versus 50% of hires in non-AI roles. articles.contentSnippet: Google made a sturdy phone, but there is increasing competition in the foldable world.
articles.fullContent: It’s strange to write this review when the world is focused on the passport-sized iPhone Duo, and China-based companies are busy releasing wide foldables with a similar design. Google, however, stuck to its guns this year and produced a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which is pretty much similar to last year’s foldable. The changes involve a lighter design, a brighter display, better wireless charging, and an updated camera sensor. The new olive color looks subtle but gorgeous, so that’s a bonus. However, with all the options out there, the device might not attract people who might be looking to buy their first foldable — unless they’re serious Pixel fans. Nonetheless, I have enjoyed using the device because the Pixel 11 Pro Fold’s cameras are competent enough, even if they aren’t a match for the Pixel 11 Pro’s setup, and the screen is nice to use despite the very visible crease. Design The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is 5mm thick when unfolded (vs 5.2mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold) and 10.1mm thick when folded (vs 10.8 mm of the Pixel 10 Pro Fold). This one is for the spec sheet because you might not feel as much difference. Despite this, the phone is not as thin as a device like the Honor V6 Magic. The difference you might notice — if you hold both this year’s and last year’s foldables — is that the new device is 19 grams lighter. But if you are buying a new device or switching from another foldable, it’s barely noticeable. The Pixel 10 Pro Fold was already a sturdy device. With this year’s version, the company claims to have increased durability by three times. Plus, there is a new glass-ceramic cover and a glass-fiber composite back cover to take up any impact. My Pixel 10 fell a few times from the table and from my pocket, but there wasn’t any visible dent or scratch. Well done, Google. Image Credits: Ivan MehtaImage Credits:Ivan Mehta One drawback of a strong hinge is that you can’t unfold the 11 Pro Fold with one hand, and that’s by design. The outer display is ever so slightly bigger, but the more observable change is the 3,600-nit display that is an upgrade from last year’s 3,000-nit peak display. This means that you can use the phone in bright conditions better. Google’s foldable still has a very visible crease in an age where phone makers like Oppo and Honor have managed to reduce the visibility significantly. The crease is more pronounced in bright light, given there is no reflective display on the device. Image Credits: Ivan MehtaImage Credits:Ivan Mehta On the back, there is the new HiLight indicator, which still lights up only for calls from your favourite contacts, and when you are talking with Gemini hands-free. There isn’t much to talk about this feature beyond that. Software and AI Reading and watching videos on a foldable is still fun, though a wide foldable might show an edge on videos. For instance, Gmail, being a Google app, lets you see your inbox on one side and a particular email on the other. This can help you get through emails faster. articles.title: Here’s what ‘renoa’ — the first new fiber in 25 years — feels like
articles.contentSnippet: Startup Everbloom's new material, renoa, is the first new fiber in 25 years, and it feels very familiar.
articles.fullContent: Sometimes it seems like everyone — and every occasion — demands cashmere these days. Numerous brands sell cashmere sweaters, from Bruno Cucinelli’s $7,900 cable knit cardigan to Quince’s $50 crewneck. Menswear company Loro Piana has made cashmere a cornerstone of its lineup, helping to drive the LVMH division’s valuation above €11 billion. There are even cashmere running shirts. But as cashmere has spread throughout the fashion industry, it’s not for everyone. It’s still relatively expensive, hard to care for, and environmental fraught. The goats that produce cashmere have been trashing rangelands across Central Asia. That may change, though. I recently experienced an alternative fiber called renoa, developed by a startup called Everbloom, that’s washable and promises to be more affordable. It could bring the cashmere experience, via a substitute material, to more products and people. Everbloom has made a number of sample items using renoa, including this glove and scarf. The scarf has been washed and dried in a tumble dryer.Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch Renoa is made from sources of waste protein, including cashmere and wool scraps as well as down and feather “lint” leftover from the bedding industry. Everbloom processes the waste into a powder and blends it with a biodegradable biopolymer, and the combination is then extruded to the right length and diameter to mimic specific natural fibers. Renoa was recently approved as the first new fiber classification in 25 years by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission, which regulates fiber labeling in the U.S. Everbloom has been developing the new fiber for three years, and is currently in the process of scaling up. The startup developed its own AI model for material science, and a cashmere substitute is the first product. Last month, I stopped by Everbloom’s headquarters in New York City, which sits 15 floors above 5th Avenue, kitty corner from Bryant Park. There, co-founder and CEO Sim Gulati walked me through a range of products made with its company’s cashmere-like renoa, including a crewneck sweater, a pair of knit gloves, and a scarf. The sweater and gloves were soft and light, but the scarf was the most notable. It didn’t look like much, but it had been through the kind of hell and back that a pure cashmere scarf wouldn’t survive. It was a custom item that Everbloom had knit to test renoa, and Gulati had been wearing and washing it for months, including a trip through the tumble dryer before I saw it. It wasn’t pilled, and Gulati said it hadn’t shrunk, either. Waste feathers (left) are ground into a powder (second from left) and combined with a biopolymer to make pellets ready for an extruder (second from right).Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch Everbloom is currently working with a range of companies to get renoa into consumer products. The first are likely to feature renoa as a blended fiber, making up around 20% of the material in a cashmere sweater, for example. The first product is expected to hit the market in the second quarter of 2027 Gulati said. The 80/20 cashmere-renoa blend that I felt was extremely close to the real thing, and Gulati said that additional finishing that accompanies commercial garments should eliminate any differences without compromising the washability and stability of the garment. After my visit, I kept thinking about various items in my closet that could benefit from those features. When renoa lands on shelves next year, I’ll be keeping an eye out for it. articles.fullContent: When I first heard about the new $149 HomePod Mini 2 at Apple’s Welcome Home event last month, I was disappointed. It’s been six years since Apple launched its entry-level smart speaker, and all it got in the second gen was a chip bump, some color glowy stuff, and better AirPlay? For $50 more than the original, which launched at $99, Apple didn’t even upgrade the sound system. It felt like the company phoned this one in.Now that I’ve got my hands on a couple and set them up in my home office, I’m more enthused. The Mini 2 is so much faster than the first-gen Mini, playing music in a few seconds and responding to smart home commands just as quickly. If you’re fed up with standing over your HomePod waiting for it to finally do what you asked, then that alone is worth the upgrade.Here are my three favorite features of the new Mini 2 after spending a couple days with it, and my one big disappointment.Siri is much snappier and much less chattyThe biggest upgrade for the Mini 2 is Siri AI, but that isn’t available yet. Apple says it’s coming “later” in a software update. However, the basic smart voice assistant has definitely improved. Siri on the Mini 2 is much snappier than on the first-gen Mini, regularly responding in under three seconds. This is thanks to a newer, faster processor (the S10, up from the S5) and Wi-Fi 6E support (up from Wi-Fi 4).When I asked Siri to play Taylor Swift, a song started in a couple of seconds. It correctly told me who won this year’s World Series in under two seconds, and turned off the light or opened the shades in under three seconds.That’s a huge improvement over the up to 10 seconds I often have to wait for Siri to get things done on the first-gen Mini. However, asking something harder, like who will win the US midterm elections, still brings up the familiar offer to look at some web results on my iPhone. As I said, Siri AI isn’t here yet.The other new behavior I am really enjoying is that when I ask Siri to perform a smart home action, such as open the shades or turn on the lights, instead of “OK, Jen,” or “One sec,” followed by a wordy confirmation of the action that I often get on the first-gen Mini, the Mini 2 just does it and doesn’t talk back. It’s not silent for every action, but it’s quiet enough to be a noticeable improvement.This Mini is gorgeous in green and sounds greatThe green color is divine. This is the prettiest small smart speaker I’ve seen — and I’ve tried them all.Yes, Amazon’s Echo Dot Max’s purple is fun, the Google Home Speaker’s pale green is elegant, but Apple’s deep green is seriously sophisticated. It’s a color that fits in really well in various places around my home, and I’m so glad the company finally released a green option. articles.fullContent: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the biggest game releases of the year, follow Andrew Webster. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepbackhere.How it startedThe two biggest games of 2026 are set to launch just a few weeks apart in November.On the one side you have the behemoth that is Grand Theft Auto VI, an experience 13 years in the making, and the sequel to one of the best-selling games in history. Its predecessor, GTA V, has sold a staggering 230 million copies since it launched in 2013, and was re-released across three generations of consoles. Developer Rockstar is a pioneer in the realm of open-world games, dating back to GTA III, and the scale and ambitions of those worlds have steadily grown since then. With GTA V and later Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio’s ideas reached a new level of realism. And the sixth GTA looks poised to eclipse them both, which has created an unprecedented level of demand.Analyst firm Circana estimates that 29 percent of gamers in the US intend to buy the game, with demand so large it could boost flagging console sales. “Many consumers who have yet to upgrade to a current-generation console may choose to purchase a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series specifically to play the title,” analyst Mat Piscatella says in a statement. GTA VI’s reach is so vast that almost every other major game launched early to avoid it.The one exception is Nintendo. The company’s tentpole release for the holidays, and its next major exclusive for the Switch 2, is a lavish remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.The release is notable for a few reasons. For one thing, it’s an attempt from Nintendo to modernize one of the most influential and beloved games in its long history. The original Ocarina of Time was the world’s first introduction to a 3D iteration of Hyrule, which, in turn, made it an early glimpse at what was possible in three-dimensional spaces, laying a blueprint for countless games that came afterward. Nintendo has since expanded on that, turning Switch-era adventures Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom into wide-open adventures designed for player creativity. They went on to become some of the best-selling games for Nintendo’s most successful console.Ocarina of Time’s launch also comes just ahead of a live-action Zelda movie in 2027, which could catapult the franchise to a new level of prominence. That’s why Nintendo is seemingly the only company unafraid of competing with GTA.These aren’t just two blockbuster games – they’re two series with the pull to make this a real cultural moment, akin to “Barbenheimer” but for video games. articles.fullContent: A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn.Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law.“The concern here is that data center developers will find a way to shoehorn their projects into the definition of an essential project and then get to take advantage of … the fast-track review that it’ll create,” says Fernando Gaytan, a senior attorney at the nonprofit environmental law organization Earthjustice, which opposes Prop 45. “Communities get cut out of the conversation.”“Communities get cut out of the conversation.”Prop 45 would loosen standards for certain projects subject to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA). CEQA requires state agencies to perform environmental reviews and work with project developers to find ways to limit any harmful impacts to the environment and public health. Crucially, CEQA also mandates that state agencies gather community input and consider public comment before issuing any approvals.Specifically, Prop 45 would create a 365-day deadline for agencies to complete the environmental impact report for a project. It also stipulates that any legal challenges would need to be settled within 270 days. It would only allow for 45 days of public comment, and it would only require state agencies and developers to consult with Native American tribes that have been federally recognized. CEQA as it’s currently written sets a minimum rather than a maximum number of days for public review, and mandates consultation with tribes that might be impacted by a project even if they’re not formally recognized by the federal government as having “government-to-government” relations with the US.During the CEQA review process, state agencies develop alternatives that developers can take to mitigate environmental and health risks. Prop 45 would turn that on its head, making developers responsible for coming up with a single alternative project plan for regulators to consider. The proposition would also strip away an agency’s authority to repeatedly ask a developer for more information about a proposed project; state regulators would need to specify all the information a company is required to provide at the start of the application process.On top of all that, Prop 45 would bar courts from halting a project altogether even if it finds that the regulatory agency failed to correctly comply with CEQA. The judge would only have the ability to pause specific parts of a project that are problematic, rather than forcing a full stop to construction. That’s the piece that’s most egregious for Gaytan. “It’s hard to undo harms once you’ve already started a project,” he says.Data centers are a hot-button election issue for midterms across the US and have become a point of contention for Prop 45 as well. articles.title: The agentic web is here
articles.contentSnippet: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. articles.fullContent: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web”: an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book a physical therapy appointment for their mother, making sure it would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars. At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent and OpenAI’s Dots are logging record downloads and being given access to people’s bank accounts and email inboxes, and Anthropic launched a research preview of its own Claude Duet agent in October. And in a worrying incident, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their badly protected sandbox and caused havoc on the open web. Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, an associate professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place for humans that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus. They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse hundreds of sites in just a few seconds, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight. As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. articles.title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
articles.fullContent: 1st November 2026 I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it. Running uv run pytest etc tends to leave uv.lock files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore and so do not get committed to my repositories. But... sometimes that uv.lock pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today: error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1` cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14) Deleting that file and running uv run pytest again usually fixes the problem.

There are obvious economic pressures pushing them down; mostly AI.
But also some pushing them up; AI makes the transition from college student -> Junior significantly harder, Junior -> Senior is also challenging. AI is scaring away some students, etc.
What's your estimate?
